Kamat, Professor, Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, University of Michigan E-mail: vkamat@umich.edu SUMMARY: The widespread adoption of Building Information Modeling (BIM) and the recent emergence of Internet of Things (IoT) applications offer several new insights and decision-making capabilities throughout the life cycle of the built environment. In recent years, the ability of real-time connectivity to online sensors deployed in an environment has led to the emergence of the concept of the Digital Twin of the built environment. Digital Twins aim to achieve synchronization of the real world with a virtual platform for seamless management and control of the construction process, facility management, environment monitoring, and other life cycle processes in the built environment. However, research in Digital Twins for the built environment is still in its nascent stages and there is a need to understand the advances in the underlying enabling technologies and establish a convergent context for ongoing and future research. This paper conducted a systematic review to identify the development of the emerging technologies facilitating the evolution of BIM to Digital Twins in built environment applications. A total of 100 related papers including 23 review papers were selected and reviewed. In order to systematically classify the reviewed studies, the authors developed a five-level ladder categorization system based on the building life cycle to reflect the current state-of-the-art in Digital Twin applications. In each level of this taxonomy, applications were further categorized based on their research domains (e.g., construction process, building energy performance, indoor environment monitoring). In addition, the current state-of-art in technologies enabling Digital Twins was also summarized from the reviewed literature. It was found that most of the prior studies conducted thus far have not fully exploited or realized the envisioned concept of the Digital Twin, and thus classify under the earlier ladder categories. Based on the analysis of the reviewed work and the trends in ongoing research, the authors propose a concept of an advanced Digital Twin for building management as a baseline for further studies. INTRODUCTION The lifecycle of a building primarily consists of the design, construction, operation, maintenance, and end of life stages where each stage can be divided into superimposed information layers that require efficient information exchange strategies for interoperability across all lifecycle stages (Vanlande et al. 2008). For example, information regarding design details needs to be exchanged between different engineering team members during the design stage, and different stakeholders need to communicate design and construction progress with each other during the construction phase (Hooper and Ekholm 2010). In addition, the building operation and facility management teams need to obtain feedback from the building facilities and occupants during operation (Das et al. 2015, Tang et al. 2020). A significant effort must therefore be invested to achieve efficient information update and exchange throughout a building's life cycle. Starting from Computer-aided Design (CAD), tools for building design and management have evolved for decades. The term "Building Information Model" was first proposed in the early 90s (van Nederveen and Tolman 1992), which was later termed "Building Information Modeling (BIM)" and has attracted much attention and become widespread in the past decades (Li et al. 2017). As a 3D digital representation of buildings, a BIM model contains both geometric and semantic information of the building elements (Eastman et al. 2011).. Due to the sharable and consistent database, BIM makes the seamless collaboration between AEC (architecture, engineering, and construction) professionals possible and thus has been widely applied in building life cycle management, including the design stage (Oh et al. 2011, Afsari et al. 2019), construction process (Azhar et al. 2008, Singh et al. 2018, Deng et al. 2019, Deng et al. 2021) as well as operating phases (Bahar et al. 2013, Soust-Verdaguer et al. 2017). fetched_contents.text: What is a digital twin? A digital twin is a virtual representation of a physical object or system that uses real-time data to accurately reflect its real-world counterpart’s behavior, performance and conditions. Digital twins enable continuous monitoring, simulation and analysis of an object, product or system over the course of its lifecycle, from design and production to maintenance and decommissioning. They can also incorporate external processes and critical variables that affect an asset’s performance. A key feature is real-time, two-way data exchange between the object and its virtual replica, helping ensure that simulated conditions accurately reflect the physical world. Enterprises can also connect multiple digital twins to model more complex systems in service of a larger digital transformation or Industry 4.0 strategy. By providing insight into how an object functions in the present—and projecting how it might behave in future scenarios—digital twins help organizations improve efficiency, accelerate innovation and make data-driven, informed decisions. Common use cases include process optimization, predictive maintenance, supply chain optimization and product development. Many modern digital twin providers, including Siemens, General Electric, Nvidia, IBM, Bentley and Microsoft, offer a full suite of services. Packages might include hardware layers (such as sensor kits), data processors, synchronization services, simulation engines, analytics platforms and visualization dashboards. But enterprises with more specialized applications might instead take a modular approach, choosing several services to match their needs. Digital twins can represent virtually any object, from buildings and bridges to cars, airplanes, historical artifacts and even the earth. They might also model complex systems such as traffic patterns, weather events, healthcare treatment plans and factory operations. Finally, in more experimental contexts, digital twins might be based on real or imagined people, complete with modeled voice, appearance and personality traits. Digital twins are now widely used across industries: A 2023 Strategic Market Research study found that roughly 75% of businesses employ them in some capacity. These initiatives can be costly and resource-intensive. But for many enterprises, they are worth the investment: 92% of companies who deploy digital twins report returns above 10%, while over half report at least 20% return on investment, according to a 2025 Hexagon survey. While digital twin workflows vary widely across industries and applications, most include these fundamental steps: Data collection An enterprise might begin by equipping a physical object with an array of sensors, which capture its performance, condition and operating environment. In IoT contexts, an organization might deploy “smart objects,” which often come preinstalled with built-in sensors that can continually collect and share data. In IT settings, teams can build digital representations of applications, software and computers (virtual machines) using virtualization technologies. They can then deploy software agents to collect data at or near the digital asset for monitoring and analysis. Virtual modeling A virtual model is a digital replica of an object or system, built using the data gathered from its real-life counterpart. It is embedded with key attributes that help it realistically react to variables such as environmental conditions and interactions with related systems. For example, a digital twin of an airplane turbine not only simulates wear and failure at the same rate as it’s real-life counterpart but also accounts for aerodynamic forces during flight and the influence of connected engine and hydraulic components. This detailed modeling helps ensure that the digital twin can reliably simulate how its real-life counterpart might respond under a range of conditions. Live data integration Live data integration enables continuous, real-time communication between the digital twin and its physical counterpart. Enterprises often automate the data exchange process, freeing them up to tackle higher-level strategic tasks. The five-level ladder taxonomy is best understood as a progression through building life cycle stages rather than a fixed set of discrete categories, and the evidence consistently points to Deng et al.’s systematic review as the source for the formal structure [N1-R1][N1-F1][N1-F2]. The taxonomy is explicitly described as a “five-level ladder categorization system based on the building life cycle” [N1-F1], and the level names are named and ordered in the source excerpt as:

- **Level 1 – BIM**
- **Level 2 – BIM-supported simulations**
- **Level 3 – BIM integrated with IoT**
- **Level 4 – BIM integrated with artificial intelligence**
- **Level 5 – advanced Digital Twin** [N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-R2][N4-R4]

This ordering reflects the transition from BIM as the foundational digital representation to increasingly connected, data-driven, and intelligent representations of the built environment. The first level is BIM itself, which serves as the baseline digital model and collaborative platform for construction and facility management [N1-F1]. The second level expands BIM with simulations, indicating that the model is no longer just a static representation but one that supports analysis and decision-making across the design and construction process [N1-F1]. The third level adds IoT integration, which introduces live data from sensors and real-time feedback to the model [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The fourth level incorporates artificial intelligence, suggesting the model can process and learn from data to improve predictions and control [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The fifth level is the advanced Digital Twin, which represents the most mature form of the taxonomy and aligns with the authors’ proposal for an advanced Digital Twin for building management [N1-F1][N1-F2][N4-R4].

The taxonomy is explicitly framed as a progression rather than a fixed set. Deng et al. note that the authors developed the ladder to “reflect the current state-of-the-art in Digital Twin applications” and that most prior studies have not fully realized the envisioned concept, so they classify them under earlier ladder categories [N1-F1]. This means the levels are meant to be read as a developmental sequence: each level builds on the prior one by adding new capabilities such as simulation, live data, IoT, AI, and finally advanced monitoring and control [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The review also emphasizes that the taxonomy is based on the building life cycle and is used to classify reviewed studies by research domain, which reinforces that the levels are part of a lifecycle-oriented transition rather than isolated stages [N1-F1]. Overall, the taxonomy is a ladder of increasing sophistication and connectivity, with BIM as the starting point and the final level representing the closest approximation to the full Digital Twin concept [N1-F1][N1-F2][N4-R4].

The evidence states that BIM is a “3D digital representation of buildings” containing both geometric and semantic information, and that it enables “seamless collaboration between AEC professionals” [N1-F1]. This suggests that BIM requires accurate geometric and semantic fidelity, strong interoperability, and a collaborative process that spans design, construction, and operation [N1-F1]. The level is also tied to the broader life-cycle context, which implies that data quality must be sufficient to support multiple stages rather than just one [N1-F1].

At **Level 2 – BIM-supported simulations**, the model is extended to support simulation and analysis. The evidence indicates that the level includes BIM-supported simulations and that prior studies are categorized under earlier ladder categories [N1-F1][N1-F2]. This implies that data quality and model fidelity must be sufficient to run meaningful simulations, such as energy or thermal analysis, and that the model must be interoperable enough to exchange simulation inputs and outputs across disciplines [N1-F1]. Collaboration and process changes here likely involve integrating simulation results into decision-making and operations [N1-F1][N1-F2].

At **Level 3 – BIM integrated with IoT**, live data becomes central. The evidence notes that the third level is “BIM integrated with IoT” and that the authors developed the taxonomy to reflect Digital Twin applications [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The IBM Digital Twin definition also emphasizes real-time data exchange, continuous monitoring, and a feedback loop between the physical and virtual worlds [N5-F3]. This means that data quality and model fidelity must improve to handle live sensor data, and that interoperability must extend to IoT devices and systems. Process changes at this level likely include real-time feedback, operational monitoring, and more dynamic collaboration between teams and systems [N1-F1][N5-F3].

At **Level 4 – BIM integrated with artificial intelligence**, the model becomes more predictive and adaptive. The evidence indicates that this level is “BIM integrated with artificial intelligence” [N1-F1][N1-F2], and the IBM material describes digital twins as enabling simulation, analysis, and predictive scenarios [N5-F3]. This suggests that model fidelity must be high enough to support AI-driven analysis and that the system must integrate analytics, machine learning, and feedback loops. Collaboration and interoperability would expand to include AI models, data pipelines, and simulation engines [N5-F3]. Live data and real-time feedback remain important, but they are now combined with predictive and adaptive capabilities [N5-F3].

At **Level 5 – advanced Digital Twin**, the system reaches the highest maturity in the taxonomy. The evidence states that the fifth level is an advanced Digital Twin for building management and that most prior studies fall into earlier categories [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The IBM definition further describes digital twins as enabling continuous monitoring, simulation, analysis, and two-way data exchange over the entire lifecycle [N5-F3]. This means that data quality and model fidelity must be extremely high, with live data, historical data, and simulation capabilities tightly integrated. Collaboration and interoperability would span the entire organization and supply chain, while process changes include predictive maintenance, optimization, and real-time decision-making [N5-F3]. The role of live data, simulation, and real-time feedback is therefore most mature at this level: the system continuously synchronizes with the physical world, supports simulation-based experimentation, and provides actionable feedback [N5-F3].

Overall, the levels show a clear progression from a static, collaborative model (Level 1) to a dynamic, data-driven, and intelligent system (Level 5). The technical features move from basic geometric/semantic BIM to simulation, then to live IoT data, then to AI-enhanced analysis, and finally to full Digital Twin capabilities with continuous monitoring and feedback [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F3].

Alternative taxonomies pose a risk of confusion because they use similar terms but define maturity or progression differently. The evidence shows that several common taxonomies exist, including 5-Dimensions, 5-levels maturity, and operational-level models, and they differ from the BIM-to-Digital-Twin five-level ladder in both structure and emphasis [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R4][N3-R5][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R4][N6-R5].

One common alternative is the **5-Dimensions** approach. Akila 3D describes digital twins as having up to five dimensions of functionality ranging from static to predictive [N3-R1]. The same source also links this to a broader taxonomy of five dimensions, which suggests a conceptual framework rather than a lifecycle-based ladder [N3-R1]. The evidence also points to a 5-Dimensional Definition for a Manufacturing Digital Twin [N3-R2] and a 5-Dimension Cross-Industry Digital Twin Applications paper [N3-R5], indicating that this taxonomy is industry-focused and dimension-based rather than life-cycle or BIM-driven [N3-R2][N3-R5]. This differs from the BIM-to-Digital-Twin ladder, which is explicitly tied to building life cycle stages and BIM as the starting point [N1-F1][N1-F2].

Another common alternative is **5-levels maturity**. The evidence includes a maturity assessment model with five maturity levels, twelve maturity dimensions, and 50 sub-dimensions [N6-R1]. It also points to IBM’s Digital Twin Maturity Model, which includes five stages: look-alike, static, dynamic, interactive, and extended [N6-R4]. A LinkedIn source describes a five-level maturity model from Level 0 to Level 5, with levels including no representation, static models, connected data systems, context-aware systems, and beyond [N6-R5]. These maturity taxonomies differ from the BIM ladder because they are maturity-based rather than lifecycle-based, and they often focus on organizational or system maturity rather than the specific BIM-to-Digital-Twin transition [N6-R1][N6-R4][N6-R5].

A third alternative is **operational-level** or **stage-level** taxonomies. The evidence includes a paper describing technologies as a digital twin system architecture with five development layers, including data acquisition, data transmission, and other layers [N5-R1]. This is not the same as the BIM ladder, because it is a system architecture taxonomy rather than a lifecycle taxonomy based on BIM [N5-R1]. It also points to the IBM Digital Twin definition, which emphasizes live data, simulation, analysis, and real-time feedback across the lifecycle [N5-F3]. This shows that operational or stage-level taxonomies can be confused with the BIM ladder if one assumes they are lifecycle-based, but the evidence indicates they are often more technical or maturity-oriented [N5-R1][N5-F3].

The risk of confusion is clear. The BIM-to-Digital-Twin five-level ladder is explicitly tied to building life cycle stages and BIM as the first level [N1-F1][N1-F2]. In contrast, 5-Dimensions models focus on functionality, maturity models emphasize organizational or system maturity, and system-architecture models emphasize technical layers [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5][N6-R1][N6-R4][N6-R5]. Confusing them can mislead users into thinking that the BIM ladder is a generic maturity model or a functional taxonomy, when it is actually a lifecycle-specific BIM-to-Digital-Twin progression [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The evidence therefore supports caution: when discussing Digital Twins, it is important to distinguish between lifecycle-based taxonomies, maturity-based taxonomies, and dimension-based taxonomies, because they answer different questions and have different implications for implementation [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R5][N6-R1][N6-R4][N6-R5].

## What are the stages and key characteristics of the five-level ladder taxonomy that describes the transition from BIM to Digital Twin?

The five-level ladder taxonomy is a lifecycle-oriented framework for understanding the evolution of building representations from **BIM** to **Digital Twin**. It is best understood not as a fixed set of discrete categories, but as a **progression through building life cycle stages** [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The formal source in the evidence is Deng et al.’s systematic review, which explicitly describes the taxonomy as a **“five-level ladder categorization system based on the building life cycle”** [N1-R1][N1-F1][N1-F2]. The evidence also provides the named and ordered levels:

- **Level 1 – BIM**
- **Level 2 – BIM-supported simulations**
- **Level 3 – BIM integrated with IoT**
- **Level 4 – BIM integrated with artificial intelligence**
- **Level 5 – advanced Digital Twin** [N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-R2][N4-R4]

This ordering reflects a clear developmental path: the lowest level is BIM, and each subsequent level adds a new capability—simulation, IoT, AI, and finally advanced Digital Twin functionality [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The authors note that the taxonomy was developed to reflect the **current state-of-the-art in Digital Twin applications**, and that many prior studies have not fully realized the envisioned concept, so they classify them under earlier ladder categories [N1-F1]. This means the levels are meant to be read as a **ladder of increasing sophistication and connectivity**, not as a rigid sequence in which every project must pass through every level [N1-F1][N1-F2].

---

## 1. Stage-by-stage description of the taxonomy

### Level 1 – BIM
At the lowest level, the system is **BIM itself**. The evidence describes BIM as a **“3D digital representation of buildings”** containing both **geometric and semantic information** [N1-F1]. It is the foundational digital model and collaborative platform for the built environment. BIM supports **seamless collaboration between AEC professionals** and is used across design, construction, and operation [N1-F1]. In the taxonomy, BIM is the starting point because it provides the shared database, model fidelity, and collaborative framework that higher levels build on [N1-F1][N1-F2].

### Level 2 – BIM-supported simulations
This level extends BIM with **simulation and analysis capabilities**. The evidence states that the taxonomy includes **BIM-supported simulations**, and that prior studies are categorized under earlier ladder categories [N1-F1][N1-F2]. This means the model must be sufficient to support meaningful simulations, such as energy or thermal analysis, and the system must be interoperable enough to exchange simulation inputs and outputs across disciplines [N1-F1]. At this stage, the transition is not just about data, but about using BIM to support decision-making and operational analysis [N1-F1][N1-F2].

### Level 3 – BIM integrated with IoT
The third level introduces **live data** and real-time feedback. The evidence notes that this level is **“BIM integrated with IoT”**, and that the taxonomy reflects Digital Twin applications [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The IBM Digital Twin definition also emphasizes **continuous monitoring, real-time data exchange, and a feedback loop** between the physical and virtual worlds [N5-F3]. At this stage, the model is no longer static; it becomes connected to sensors and other live data sources, and its fidelity must improve to handle sensor data and real-time synchronization [N1-F1][N5-F3].

### Level 4 – BIM integrated with artificial intelligence
The fourth level adds **artificial intelligence** to the system. The evidence explicitly states that this level is **“BIM integrated with artificial intelligence”** [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The IBM Digital Twin definition describes digital twins as enabling **simulation, analysis, and predictive scenarios**, which supports the idea that AI enhances the model’s ability to analyze data, predict outcomes, and adapt over time [N5-F3]. This level requires high-quality data and a robust analytics pipeline, with collaboration and interoperability expanding to include AI models and simulation engines [N5-F3].

### Level 5 – advanced Digital Twin
The fifth and highest level is the **advanced Digital Twin** for building management. The evidence states that the fifth level is an advanced Digital Twin and that many prior studies fall into earlier categories [N1-F1][N1-F2]. IBM describes digital twins as enabling **continuous monitoring, simulation, analysis, and two-way data exchange over the entire lifecycle** [N5-F3]. At this stage, the system is highly synchronized with the real world, supports predictive and adaptive behavior, and integrates live data, historical data, and simulation across the full lifecycle [N5-F3]. This is the closest approximation to the full Digital Twin concept in the taxonomy [N1-F1][N1-F2].

---

## 2. Key characteristics and technical features of each level

The levels move from a **static, collaborative model** at Level 1 to a **dynamic, data-driven, and intelligent system** at Level 5 [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The key characteristics include:

### Data quality and model fidelity
- **Level 1 – BIM**: Requires accurate **geometric and semantic fidelity** to support collaboration and lifecycle management [N1-F1].
- **Level 2 – BIM-supported simulations**: Requires data quality sufficient to run meaningful simulations and support analysis [N1-F1][N1-F2].
- **Level 3 – BIM integrated with IoT**: Requires the model to handle **live sensor data** and maintain synchronization with the physical world [N1-F1][N5-F3].
- **Level 4 – BIM integrated with artificial intelligence**: Requires high-quality data to support AI-driven analysis, machine learning, and predictive modeling [N5-F3].
- **Level 5 – advanced Digital Twin**: Requires extremely high data quality and model fidelity, with live data, historical data, and simulation tightly integrated [N5-F3].

### Collaboration, interoperability, and process changes
- **Level 1 – BIM**: Supports **seamless collaboration** across AEC professionals and is the foundation for interoperability [N1-F1].
- **Level 2 – BIM-supported simulations**: Changes process to include simulation-based decision-making and cross-disciplinary interoperability [N1-F1][N1-F2].
- **Level 3 – BIM integrated with IoT**: Introduces real-time collaboration with IoT devices and live data flows [N1-F1][N5-F3].
- **Level 4 – BIM integrated with artificial intelligence**: Expands collaboration and interoperability to include AI models, analytics pipelines, and simulation engines [N5-F3].
- **Level 5 – advanced Digital Twin**: Supports full lifecycle collaboration, with data, analytics, and control integrated across the organization [N1-F1][N5-F3].

### Role of live data, simulation, and real-time feedback
- **Level 1 – BIM**: Live data is not central, but the model is the basis for later live data integration [N1-F1].
- **Level 2 – BIM-supported simulations**: Simulation becomes a core feature, but real-time feedback is still limited [N1-F1][N1-F2].
- **Level 3 – BIM integrated with IoT**: Live data and real-time feedback become central, with continuous monitoring and synchronization [N1-F1][N5-F3].
- **Level 4 – BIM integrated with artificial intelligence**: Simulation and feedback are enhanced by AI, enabling predictive and adaptive behavior [N5-F3].
- **Level 5 – advanced Digital Twin**: Live data, simulation, and real-time feedback are fully integrated, with continuous two-way exchange and predictive control [N5-F3].

---

## 3. How BIM fits into the lowest level and supports higher levels

BIM is the **lowest level** in the taxonomy and the **foundation for higher levels**. The evidence makes this explicit: Deng et al. describe the five-level ladder as a categorization system based on the **building life cycle**, and they explicitly state that **Level 1 is BIM** [N1-F1][N1-F2]. They also emphasize that BIM is a 3D digital representation containing geometric and semantic information, and that it enables **seamless collaboration between AEC professionals** [N1-F1]. This means BIM provides the initial digital model, shared database, and collaborative framework that later stages add on top of [N1-F1][N1-F2].

The transition from BIM to Digital Twin is supported by the fact that BIM is already widely used in design, construction, and operation [N1-F1]. The taxonomy is built on the building life cycle, so the transition is not just a one-time model upgrade but a **lifecycle progression** from design through operation and maintenance [N1-F1]. The authors also note that most prior studies have not fully realized the envisioned Digital Twin, so they classify them under earlier ladder categories [N1-F1]. This reinforces that BIM supports higher levels by providing the foundational model and collaborative infrastructure that later stages build upon [N1-F1][N1-F2].

---

## 4. Organizational and technical barriers in the transition

The evidence indicates several **organizational and technical barriers** in the transition from BIM to Digital Twin.

### Technical barriers
- **Interoperability**: The review notes that information exchange strategies are needed for interoperability across all lifecycle stages [N1-F1]. This is a major technical barrier because BIM must support cross-disciplinary and cross-system data exchange.
- **Data quality and synchronization**: Live data and real-time feedback require high-quality data and tight synchronization between the physical and virtual worlds [N5-F3].
- **AI integration**: Moving to artificial intelligence requires not only data quality but also robust analytics pipelines, machine learning capabilities, and feedback loops [N5-F3].
- **Sensor and IoT integration**: Level 3 depends on connecting BIM to IoT devices, which introduces new technical challenges in data acquisition, transmission, and synchronization [N1-F1][N5-F3].

### Organizational barriers
- **Collaboration and change management**: BIM already supports collaboration, but the transition to Digital Twin requires more extensive cross-organizational and cross-functional coordination [N1-F1][N1-F2].
- **Organizational readiness**: The taxonomy helps explain Digital Twin maturity, but the evidence also suggests that many prior studies are still in earlier ladder categories [N1-F1]. This implies that organizational barriers may include resistance to change, lack of cross-disciplinary collaboration, and difficulty in aligning different systems and processes [N1-F1][N5-F3].

---

## 5. How the taxonomy helps explain Digital Twin maturity

The taxonomy is a useful way to explain **Digital Twin maturity** because it frames the transition as a **lifecycle progression** rather than a single point in time [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The authors’ proposal for an **advanced Digital Twin for building management** shows that the taxonomy is meant to map maturity, not prescribe a single endpoint [N1-F2]. The evidence also states that studies are classified into ladder categories based on how far they have progressed, which means the taxonomy can be used to assess where a project sits in the Digital Twin maturity curve [N1-F1].

In practical terms, the taxonomy helps explain maturity by showing that higher levels require more:
- live data and real-time feedback
- simulation and predictive capability
- AI and analytics
- cross-organizational and cross-system interoperability
- full lifecycle synchronization and control [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F3]

So, maturity is not just about having a Digital Twin; it is about how far along the BIM-to-Digital-Twin ladder a system has progressed [N1-F1][N1-F2].

---

## 6. Alternative taxonomies and why they matter

The evidence shows that several **alternative taxonomies** exist, and they pose a risk of confusion with the BIM-to-Digital-Twin five-level ladder [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R4][N3-R5][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R4][N6-R5]. The most common alternatives include:

- **5-Dimensions models**, which describe digital twins in terms of functionality ranging from static to predictive [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5].
- **5-levels maturity models**, which are maturity-based rather than lifecycle-based and often include stages such as look-alike, static, dynamic, interactive, and extended [N6-R1][N6-R4][N6-R5].
- **System-architecture taxonomies**, which describe digital twins as a layered system with development layers such as data acquisition, data transmission, and other technical layers [N5-R1].

These alternatives differ from the BIM ladder because:
- They are not explicitly tied to the **building life cycle** or **BIM as the first level** [N1-F1][N1-F2].
- They may focus on **functionality**, **maturity**, or **technical architecture** rather than the **BIM-to-Digital-Twin transition** [N3-R1][N3-R2][N6-R1][N6-R4].
- They can be confused with the BIM ladder if one assumes that all “five-level” or “five-dimensional” frameworks are lifecycle-based [N1-F1][N1-F2].

This is important because confusing the BIM ladder with a maturity model or a dimension-based taxonomy can lead to misinterpretation of what the taxonomy is meant to capture [N1-F1][N1-F2][N3-R1][N3-R2][N6-R1][N6-R4].

---

## Conclusion

The five-level ladder taxonomy describes the transition from **BIM** to **Digital Twin** as a **lifecycle progression** through five stages:

1. **BIM** – the foundational digital model and collaborative platform
2. **BIM-supported simulations** – simulation and analysis
3. **BIM integrated with IoT** – live data and real-time feedback
4. **BIM integrated with artificial intelligence** – AI-driven analysis and prediction
5. **advanced Digital Twin** – full lifecycle synchronization and control

The key characteristics are increasing **data quality**, **model fidelity**, **collaboration**, **interoperability**, and **real-time feedback**, with live data and simulation becoming progressively more central [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F3]. BIM is the lowest level and the foundation for higher levels, and the taxonomy helps explain Digital Twin maturity by showing where a project sits along the ladder [N1-F1][N1-F2].

The evidence also warns that alternative taxonomies such as **5-Dimensions**, **5-levels maturity**, and **operational-level** models can be confusing if treated as equivalent to the BIM-to-Digital-Twin ladder [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5][N6-R1][N6-R4]. The safest interpretation is that the BIM ladder is a **building lifecycle-based taxonomy**, while other taxonomies are **functionality-based**, **maturity-based**, or **system-architecture-based** [N1-F1][N1-F2][N3-R1][N6-R1].

## What are the stages and key characteristics of the five-level ladder taxonomy that describes the transition from BIM to Digital Twin?

The five-level ladder taxonomy is a lifecycle-oriented framework for understanding the evolution of building representations from **BIM** to **Digital Twin**. It is best understood not as a fixed set of discrete categories, but as a **progression through building life cycle stages** [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The formal source in the evidence is Deng et al.’s systematic review, which explicitly describes the taxonomy as a **“five-level ladder categorization system based on the building life cycle”** [N1-R1][N1-F1][N1-F2]. The evidence also provides the named and ordered levels:

- **Level 1 – BIM**
- **Level 2 – BIM-supported simulations**
- **Level 3 – BIM integrated with IoT**
- **Level 4 – BIM integrated with artificial intelligence**
- **Level 5 – advanced Digital Twin** [N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-R2][N4-R4]

This ordering reflects a clear developmental path: the lowest level is BIM, and each subsequent level adds a new capability—simulation, IoT, AI, and finally advanced Digital Twin functionality [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The authors note that the taxonomy was developed to reflect the **current state-of-the-art in Digital Twin applications**, and that many prior studies have not fully realized the envisioned concept, so they classify them under earlier ladder categories [N1-F1]. This means the levels are meant to be read as a **ladder of increasing sophistication and connectivity**, not as a rigid sequence in which every project must pass through every level [N1-F1][N1-F2].

---

## 1. Stage-by-stage description of the taxonomy

### Level 1 – BIM
At the lowest level, the system is **BIM itself**. The evidence describes BIM as a **“3D digital representation of buildings”** containing both **geometric and semantic information** [N1-F1]. It is the foundational digital model and collaborative platform for the built environment. BIM supports **seamless collaboration between AEC professionals** and is used across design, construction, and operation [N1-F1]. In the taxonomy, BIM is the starting point because it provides the shared database, model fidelity, and collaborative framework that higher levels build on [N1-F1][N1-F2].

### Level 2 – BIM-supported simulations
This level extends BIM with **simulation and analysis capabilities**. The evidence states that the taxonomy includes **BIM-supported simulations**, and that prior studies are categorized under earlier ladder categories [N1-F1][N1-F2]. This means the model must be sufficient to support meaningful simulations, such as energy or thermal analysis, and the system must be interoperable enough to exchange simulation inputs and outputs across disciplines [N1-F1]. At this stage, the transition is not just about data, but about using BIM to support decision-making and operational analysis [N1-F1][N1-F2].

### Level 3 – BIM integrated with IoT
The third level introduces **live data** and real-time feedback. The evidence notes that this level is **“BIM integrated with IoT”**, and that the taxonomy reflects Digital Twin applications [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The IBM Digital Twin definition also emphasizes **continuous monitoring, real-time data exchange, and a feedback loop** between the physical and virtual worlds [N5-F3]. At this stage, the model is no longer static; it becomes connected to sensors and other live data sources, and its fidelity must improve to handle sensor data and real-time synchronization [N1-F1][N5-F3].

### Level 4 – BIM integrated with artificial intelligence
The fourth level adds **artificial intelligence** to the system. The evidence explicitly states that this level is **“BIM integrated with artificial intelligence”** [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The IBM Digital Twin definition describes digital twins as enabling **simulation, analysis, and predictive scenarios**, which supports the idea that AI enhances the model’s ability to analyze data, predict outcomes, and adapt over time [N5-F3]. This level requires high-quality data and a robust analytics pipeline, with collaboration and interoperability expanding to include AI models and simulation engines [N5-F3].

### Level 5 – advanced Digital Twin
The fifth and highest level is the **advanced Digital Twin** for building management. The evidence states that the fifth level is an advanced Digital Twin and that many prior studies fall into earlier categories [N1-F1][N1-F2]. IBM describes digital twins as enabling **continuous monitoring, simulation, analysis, and two-way data exchange over the entire lifecycle** [N5-F3]. At this stage, the system is highly synchronized with the real world, supports predictive and adaptive behavior, and integrates live data, historical data, and simulation across the full lifecycle [N5-F3]. This is the closest approximation to the full Digital Twin concept in the taxonomy [N1-F1][N1-F2].

---

## 2. Key characteristics and technical features of each level

The levels move from a **static, collaborative model** at Level 1 to a **dynamic, data-driven, and intelligent system** at Level 5 [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The key characteristics include:

### Data quality and model fidelity
- **Level 1 – BIM**: Requires accurate **geometric and semantic fidelity** to support collaboration and lifecycle management [N1-F1].
- **Level 2 – BIM-supported simulations**: Requires data quality sufficient to run meaningful simulations and support analysis [N1-F1][N1-F2].
- **Level 3 – BIM integrated with IoT**: Requires the model to handle **live sensor data** and maintain synchronization with the physical world [N1-F1][N5-F3].
- **Level 4 – BIM integrated with artificial intelligence**: Requires high-quality data to support AI-driven analysis, machine learning, and predictive modeling [N5-F3].
- **Level 5 – advanced Digital Twin**: Requires extremely high data quality and model fidelity, with live data, historical data, and simulation tightly integrated [N5-F3].

### Collaboration, interoperability, and process changes
- **Level 1 – BIM**: Supports **seamless collaboration** across AEC professionals and is the foundation for interoperability [N1-F1].
- **Level 2 – BIM-supported simulations**: Changes process to include simulation-based decision-making and cross-disciplinary interoperability [N1-F1][N1-F2].
- **Level 3 – BIM integrated with IoT**: Introduces real-time collaboration with IoT devices and live data flows [N1-F1][N5-F3].
- **Level 4 – BIM integrated with artificial intelligence**: Expands collaboration and interoperability to include AI models, analytics pipelines, and simulation engines [N5-F3].
- **Level 5 – advanced Digital Twin**: Supports full lifecycle collaboration, with data, analytics, and control integrated across the organization [N1-F1][N5-F3].

### Role of live data, simulation, and real-time feedback
- **Level 1 – BIM**: Live data is not central, but the model is the basis for later live data integration [N1-F1].
- **Level 2 – BIM-supported simulations**: Simulation becomes a core feature, but real-time feedback is still limited [N1-F1][N1-F2].
- **Level 3 – BIM integrated with IoT**: Live data and real-time feedback become central, with continuous monitoring and synchronization [N1-F1][N5-F3].
- **Level 4 – BIM integrated with artificial intelligence**: Simulation and feedback are enhanced by AI, enabling predictive and adaptive behavior [N5-F3].
- **Level 5 – advanced Digital Twin**: Live data, simulation, and real-time feedback are fully integrated, with continuous two-way exchange and predictive control [N5-F3].

---

## 3. How BIM fits into the lowest level and supports higher levels

BIM is the **lowest level** in the taxonomy and the **foundation for higher levels**. The evidence makes this explicit: Deng et al. describe the five-level ladder as a categorization system based on the **building life cycle**, and they explicitly state that **Level 1 is BIM** [N1-F1][N1-F2]. They also emphasize that BIM is a 3D digital representation containing geometric and semantic information, and that it enables **seamless collaboration between AEC professionals** [N1-F1]. This means BIM provides the initial digital model, shared database, and collaborative framework that later stages add on top of [N1-F1][N1-F2].

The transition from BIM to Digital Twin is supported by the fact that BIM is already widely used in design, construction, and operation [N1-F1]. The taxonomy is built on the building life cycle, so the transition is not just a one-time model upgrade but a **lifecycle progression** from design through operation and maintenance [N1-F1]. The authors also note that most prior studies have not fully realized the envisioned Digital Twin, so they classify them under earlier ladder categories [N1-F1]. This reinforces that BIM supports higher levels by providing the foundational model and collaborative infrastructure that later stages build upon [N1-F1][N1-F2].

---

## 4. Organizational and technical barriers in the transition

The evidence indicates several **organizational and technical barriers** in the transition from BIM to Digital Twin.

### Technical barriers
- **Interoperability**: The review notes that information exchange strategies are needed for interoperability across all lifecycle stages [N1-F1]. This is a major technical barrier because BIM must support cross-disciplinary and cross-system data exchange.
- **Data quality and synchronization**: Live data and real-time feedback require high-quality data and tight synchronization between the physical and virtual worlds [N5-F3].
- **AI integration**: Moving to artificial intelligence requires not only data quality but also robust analytics pipelines, machine learning capabilities, and feedback loops [N5-F3].
- **Sensor and IoT integration**: Level 3 depends on connecting BIM to IoT devices, which introduces new technical challenges in data acquisition, transmission, and synchronization [N1-F1][N5-F3].

### Organizational barriers
- **Collaboration and change management**: BIM already supports collaboration, but the transition to Digital Twin requires more extensive cross-organizational and cross-functional coordination [N1-F1][N1-F2].
- **Organizational readiness**: The taxonomy helps explain Digital Twin maturity, but the evidence also suggests that many prior studies are still in earlier ladder categories [N1-F1]. This implies that organizational barriers may include resistance to change, lack of cross-disciplinary collaboration, and difficulty in aligning different systems and processes [N1-F1][N5-F3].

---

## 5. How the taxonomy helps explain Digital Twin maturity

The taxonomy is a useful way to explain **Digital Twin maturity** because it frames the transition as a **lifecycle progression** rather than a single point in time [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The authors’ proposal for an **advanced Digital Twin for building management** shows that the taxonomy is meant to map maturity, not prescribe a single endpoint [N1-F2]. The evidence also states that studies are classified into ladder categories based on how far they have progressed, which means the taxonomy can be used to assess where a project sits in the Digital Twin maturity curve [N1-F1].

In practical terms, the taxonomy helps explain maturity by showing that higher levels require more:
- live data and real-time feedback
- simulation and predictive capability
- AI and analytics
- cross-organizational and cross-system interoperability
- full lifecycle synchronization and control [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F3]

So, maturity is not just about having a Digital Twin; it is about how far along the BIM-to-Digital-Twin ladder a system has progressed [N1-F1][N1-F2].

---

## 6. Alternative taxonomies and why they matter

The evidence shows that several **alternative taxonomies** exist, and they pose a risk of confusion with the BIM-to-Digital-Twin five-level ladder [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R4][N3-R5][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R4][N6-R5]. The most common alternatives include:

- **5-Dimensions models**, which describe digital twins in terms of functionality ranging from static to predictive [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5].
- **5-levels maturity models**, which are maturity-based rather than lifecycle-based and often include stages such as look-alike, static, dynamic, interactive, and extended [N6-R1][N6-R4][N6-R5].
- **System-architecture taxonomies**, which describe digital twins as a layered system with development layers such as data acquisition, data transmission, and other technical layers [N5-R1].

These alternatives differ from the BIM ladder because:
- They are not explicitly tied to the **building life cycle** or **BIM as the first level** [N1-F1][N1-F2].
- They may focus on **functionality**, **maturity**, or **technical architecture** rather than the **BIM-to-Digital-Twin transition** [N3-R1][N3-R2][N6-R1][N6-R4].
- They can be confused with the BIM ladder if one assumes that all “five-level” or “five-dimensional” frameworks are lifecycle-based [N1-F1][N1-F2].

This is important because confusing the BIM ladder with a maturity model or a dimension-based taxonomy can lead to misinterpretation of what the taxonomy is meant to capture [N1-F1][N1-F2][N3-R1][N3-R2][N6-R1][N6-R4].

---

## Conclusion

The five-level ladder taxonomy describes the transition from **BIM** to **Digital Twin** as a **lifecycle progression** through five stages:

1. **BIM** – the foundational digital model and collaborative platform
2. **BIM-supported simulations** – simulation and analysis
3. **BIM integrated with IoT** – live data and real-time feedback
4. **BIM integrated with artificial intelligence** – AI-driven analysis and prediction
5. **advanced Digital Twin** – full lifecycle synchronization and control

The key characteristics are increasing **data quality**, **model fidelity**, **collaboration**, **interoperability**, and **real-time feedback**, with live data and simulation becoming progressively more central [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F3]. BIM is the lowest level and the foundation for higher levels, and the taxonomy helps explain Digital Twin maturity by showing where a project sits along the ladder [N1-F1][N1-F2].

The evidence also warns that alternative taxonomies such as **5-Dimensions**, **5-levels maturity**, and **operational-level** models can be confusing if treated as equivalent to the BIM-to-Digital-Twin ladder [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5][N6-R1][N6-R4]. The safest interpretation is that the BIM ladder is a **building lifecycle-based taxonomy**, while other taxonomies are **functionality-based**, **maturity-based**, or **system-architecture-based** [N1-F1][N1-F2][N3-R1][N6-R1].

## What are the stages and key characteristics of the five-level ladder taxonomy that describes the transition from BIM to Digital Twin?

The five-level ladder taxonomy is a lifecycle-oriented framework for understanding the evolution of building representations from **BIM** to **Digital Twin**. It is best understood not as a fixed set of discrete categories, but as a **progression through building life cycle stages** [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The formal source in the evidence is Deng et al.’s systematic review, which explicitly describes the taxonomy as a **“five-level ladder categorization system based on the building life cycle”** [N1-R1][N1-F1][N1-F2]. The evidence also provides the named and ordered levels:

- **Level 1 – BIM**
- **Level 2 – BIM-supported simulations**
- **Level 3 – BIM integrated with IoT**
- **Level 4 – BIM integrated with artificial intelligence**
- **Level 5 – advanced Digital Twin** [N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-R2][N4-R4]

This ordering reflects a clear developmental path: the lowest level is BIM, and each subsequent level adds a new capability—simulation, IoT, AI, and finally advanced Digital Twin functionality [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The authors note that the taxonomy was developed to reflect the **current state-of-the-art in Digital Twin applications**, and that many prior studies have not fully realized the envisioned concept, so they classify them under earlier ladder categories [N1-F1]. This means the levels are meant to be read as a **ladder of increasing sophistication and connectivity**, not as a rigid sequence in which every project must pass through every level [N1-F1][N1-F2].

---

## 1. Stage-by-stage description of the taxonomy

### Level 1 – BIM
At the lowest level, the system is **BIM itself**. The evidence describes BIM as a **“3D digital representation of buildings”** containing both **geometric and semantic information** [N1-F1]. It is the foundational digital model and collaborative platform for the built environment. BIM supports **seamless collaboration between AEC professionals** and is used across design, construction, and operation [N1-F1]. In the taxonomy, BIM is the starting point because it provides the shared database, model fidelity, and collaborative framework that higher levels build on [N1-F1][N1-F2].

### Level 2 – BIM-supported simulations
This level extends BIM with **simulation and analysis capabilities**. The evidence states that the taxonomy includes **BIM-supported simulations**, and that prior studies are categorized under earlier ladder categories [N1-F1][N1-F2]. This means the model must be sufficient to support meaningful simulations, such as energy or thermal analysis, and the system must be interoperable enough to exchange simulation inputs and outputs across disciplines [N1-F1]. At this stage, the transition is not just about data, but about using BIM to support decision-making and operational analysis [N1-F1][N1-F2].

### Level 3 – BIM integrated with IoT
The third level introduces **live data** and real-time feedback. The evidence notes that this level is **“BIM integrated with IoT”**, and that the taxonomy reflects Digital Twin applications [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The IBM Digital Twin definition also emphasizes **continuous monitoring, real-time data exchange, and a feedback loop** between the physical and virtual worlds [N5-F3]. At this stage, the model is no longer static; it becomes connected to sensors and other live data sources, and its fidelity must improve to handle sensor data and real-time synchronization [N1-F1][N5-F3].

### Level 4 – BIM integrated with artificial intelligence
The fourth level adds **artificial intelligence** to the system. The evidence explicitly states that this level is **“BIM integrated with artificial intelligence”** [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The IBM Digital Twin definition describes digital twins as enabling **simulation, analysis, and predictive scenarios**, which supports the idea that AI enhances the model’s ability to analyze data, predict outcomes, and adapt over time [N5-F3]. This level requires high-quality data and a robust analytics pipeline, with collaboration and interoperability expanding to include AI models and simulation engines [N5-F3].

### Level 5 – advanced Digital Twin
The fifth and highest level is the **advanced Digital Twin** for building management. The evidence states that the fifth level is an advanced Digital Twin and that many prior studies fall into earlier categories [N1-F1][N1-F2]. IBM describes digital twins as enabling **continuous monitoring, simulation, analysis, and two-way data exchange over the entire lifecycle** [N5-F3]. At this stage, the system is highly synchronized with the real world, supports predictive and adaptive behavior, and integrates live data, historical data, and simulation across the full lifecycle [N5-F3]. This is the closest approximation to the full Digital Twin concept in the taxonomy [N1-F1][N1-F2].

---

## 2. Key characteristics and technical features of each level

The levels move from a **static, collaborative model** at Level 1 to a **dynamic, data-driven, and intelligent system** at Level 5 [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The key characteristics include:

### Data quality and model fidelity
- **Level 1 – BIM**: Requires accurate **geometric and semantic fidelity** to support collaboration and lifecycle management [N1-F1].
- **Level 2 – BIM-supported simulations**: Requires data quality sufficient to run meaningful simulations and support analysis [N1-F1][N1-F2].
- **Level 3 – BIM integrated with IoT**: Requires the model to handle **live sensor data** and maintain synchronization with the physical world [N1-F1][N5-F3].
- **Level 4 – BIM integrated with artificial intelligence**: Requires high-quality data to support AI-driven analysis, machine learning, and predictive modeling [N5-F3].
- **Level 5 – advanced Digital Twin**: Requires extremely high data quality and model fidelity, with live data, historical data, and simulation tightly integrated [N5-F3].

### Collaboration, interoperability, and process changes
- **Level 1 – BIM**: Supports **seamless collaboration** across AEC professionals and is the foundation for interoperability [N1-F1].
- **Level 2 – BIM-supported simulations**: Changes process to include simulation-based decision-making and cross-disciplinary interoperability [N1-F1][N1-F2].
- **Level 3 – BIM integrated with IoT**: Introduces real-time collaboration with IoT devices and live data flows [N1-F1][N5-F3].
- **Level 4 – BIM integrated with artificial intelligence**: Expands collaboration and interoperability to include AI models, analytics pipelines, and simulation engines [N5-F3].
- **Level 5 – advanced Digital Twin**: Supports full lifecycle collaboration, with data, analytics, and control integrated across the organization [N1-F1][N5-F3].

### Role of live data, simulation, and real-time feedback
- **Level 1 – BIM**: Live data is not central, but the model is the basis for later live data integration [N1-F1].
- **Level 2 – BIM-supported simulations**: Simulation becomes a core feature, but real-time feedback is still limited [N1-F1][N1-F2].
- **Level 3 – BIM integrated with IoT**: Live data and real-time feedback become central, with continuous monitoring and synchronization [N1-F1][N5-F3].
- **Level 4 – BIM integrated with artificial intelligence**: Simulation and feedback are enhanced by AI, enabling predictive and adaptive behavior [N5-F3].
- **Level 5 – advanced Digital Twin**: Live data, simulation, and real-time feedback are fully integrated, with continuous two-way exchange and predictive control [N5-F3].

---

## 3. How BIM fits into the lowest level and supports higher levels

BIM is the **lowest level** in the taxonomy and the **foundation for higher levels**. The evidence makes this explicit: Deng et al. describe the five-level ladder as a categorization system based on the **building life cycle**, and they explicitly state that **Level 1 is BIM** [N1-F1][N1-F2]. They also emphasize that BIM is a 3D digital representation containing geometric and semantic information, and that it enables **seamless collaboration between AEC professionals** [N1-F1]. This means BIM provides the initial digital model, shared database, and collaborative framework that later stages add on top of [N1-F1][N1-F2].

The transition from BIM to Digital Twin is supported by the fact that BIM is already widely used in design, construction, and operation [N1-F1]. The taxonomy is built on the building life cycle, so the transition is not just a one-time model upgrade but a **lifecycle progression** from design through operation and maintenance [N1-F1]. The authors also note that most prior studies have not fully realized the envisioned Digital Twin, so they classify them under earlier ladder categories [N1-F1]. This reinforces that BIM supports higher levels by providing the foundational model and collaborative infrastructure that later stages build upon [N1-F1][N1-F2].

---

## 4. Organizational and technical barriers in the transition

The evidence indicates several **organizational and technical barriers** in the transition from BIM to Digital Twin.

### Technical barriers
- **Interoperability**: The review notes that information exchange strategies are needed for interoperability across all lifecycle stages [N1-F1]. This is a major technical barrier because BIM must support cross-disciplinary and cross-system data exchange.
- **Data quality and synchronization**: Live data and real-time feedback require high-quality data and tight synchronization between the physical and virtual worlds [N5-F3].
- **AI integration**: Moving to artificial intelligence requires not only data quality but also robust analytics pipelines, machine learning capabilities, and feedback loops [N5-F3].
- **Sensor and IoT integration**: Level 3 depends on connecting BIM to IoT devices, which introduces new technical challenges in data acquisition, transmission, and synchronization [N1-F1][N5-F3].

### Organizational barriers
- **Collaboration and change management**: BIM already supports collaboration, but the transition to Digital Twin requires more extensive cross-organizational and cross-functional coordination [N1-F1][N1-F2].
- **Organizational readiness**: The taxonomy helps explain Digital Twin maturity, but the evidence also suggests that many prior studies are still in earlier ladder categories [N1-F1]. This implies that organizational barriers may include resistance to change, lack of cross-disciplinary collaboration, and difficulty in aligning different systems and processes [N1-F1][N5-F3].

---

## 5. How the taxonomy helps explain Digital Twin maturity

The taxonomy is a useful way to explain **Digital Twin maturity** because it frames the transition as a **lifecycle progression** rather than a single point in time [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The authors’ proposal for an **advanced Digital Twin for building management** shows that the taxonomy is meant to map maturity, not prescribe a single endpoint [N1-F2]. The evidence also states that studies are classified into ladder categories based on how far they have progressed, which means the taxonomy can be used to assess where a project sits in the Digital Twin maturity curve [N1-F1].

In practical terms, the taxonomy helps explain maturity by showing that higher levels require more:
- live data and real-time feedback
- simulation and predictive capability
- AI and analytics
- cross-organizational and cross-system interoperability
- full lifecycle synchronization and control [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F3]

So, maturity is not just about having a Digital Twin; it is about how far along the BIM-to-Digital-Twin ladder a system has progressed [N1-F1][N1-F2].

---

## 6. Alternative taxonomies and why they matter

The evidence shows that several **alternative taxonomies** exist, and they pose a risk of confusion with the BIM-to-Digital-Twin five-level ladder [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R4][N3-R5][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R4][N6-R5]. The most common alternatives include:

- **5-Dimensions models**, which describe digital twins in terms of functionality ranging from static to predictive [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5].
- **5-levels maturity models**, which are maturity-based rather than lifecycle-based and often include stages such as look-alike, static, dynamic, interactive, and extended [N6-R1][N6-R4][N6-R5].
- **System-architecture taxonomies**, which describe digital twins as a layered system with development layers such as data acquisition, data transmission, and other technical layers [N5-R1].

These alternatives differ from the BIM ladder because:
- They are not explicitly tied to the **building life cycle** or **BIM as the first level** [N1-F1][N1-F2].
- They may focus on **functionality**, **maturity**, or **technical architecture** rather than the **BIM-to-Digital-Twin transition** [N3-R1][N3-R2][N6-R1][N6-R4].
- They can be confused with the BIM ladder if one assumes that all “five-level” or “five-dimensional” frameworks are lifecycle-based [N1-F1][N1-F2].

This is important because confusing the BIM ladder with a maturity model or a dimension-based taxonomy can lead to misinterpretation of what the taxonomy is meant to capture [N1-F1][N1-F2][N3-R1][N3-R2][N6-R1][N6-R4].

---

## Conclusion

The five-level ladder taxonomy describes the transition from **BIM** to **Digital Twin** as a **lifecycle progression** through five stages:

1. **BIM** – the foundational digital model and collaborative platform
2. **BIM-supported simulations** – simulation and analysis
3. **BIM integrated with IoT** – live data and real-time feedback
4. **BIM integrated with artificial intelligence** – AI-driven analysis and prediction
5. **advanced Digital Twin** – full lifecycle synchronization and control

The key characteristics are increasing **data quality**, **model fidelity**, **collaboration**, **interoperability**, and **real-time feedback**, with live data and simulation becoming progressively more central [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F3]. BIM is the lowest level and the foundation for higher levels, and the taxonomy helps explain Digital Twin maturity by showing where a project sits along the ladder [N1-F1][N1-F2].

The evidence also warns that alternative taxonomies such as **5-Dimensions**, **5-levels maturity**, and **operational-level** models can be confusing if treated as equivalent to the BIM-to-Digital-Twin ladder [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5][N6-R1][N6-R4]. The safest interpretation is that the BIM ladder is a **building lifecycle-based taxonomy**, while other taxonomies are **functionality-based**, **maturity-based**, or **system-architecture-based** [N1-F1][N1-F2][N3-R1][N6-R1].

- **Level 3 – BIM integrated with IoT**: Introduces real-time collaboration with IoT devices and live data flows [N1-F1][N5-F3].
- **Level 4 – BIM integrated with artificial intelligence**: Expands collaboration and interoperability to include AI models, analytics pipelines, and simulation engines [N5-F3].
- **Level 5 – advanced Digital Twin**: Supports full lifecycle collaboration, with data, analytics, and control integrated across the organization [N1-F1][N5-F3].

### Role of live data, simulation, and real-time feedback
- **Level 1 – BIM**: Live data is not central, but the model is the basis for later live data integration [N1-F1].
- **Level 2 – BIM-supported simulations**: Simulation becomes a core feature, but real-time feedback is still limited [N1-F1][N1-F2].
- **Level 3 – BIM integrated with IoT**: Live data and real-time feedback become central, with continuous monitoring and synchronization [N1-F1][N5-F3].
- **Level 4 – BIM integrated with artificial intelligence**: Simulation and feedback are enhanced by AI, enabling predictive and adaptive behavior [N5-F3].
- **Level 5 – advanced Digital Twin**: Live data, simulation, and real-time feedback are fully integrated, with continuous two-way exchange and predictive control [N5-F3].

---

## 3. How BIM fits into the lowest level and supports higher levels

BIM is the **lowest level** in the taxonomy and the **foundation for higher levels**. The evidence makes this explicit: Deng et al. describe the five-level ladder as a categorization system based on the **building life cycle**, and they explicitly state that **Level 1 is BIM** [N1-F1][N1-F2]. They also emphasize that BIM is a 3D digital representation containing geometric and semantic information, and that it enables **seamless collaboration between AEC professionals** [N1-F1]. This means BIM provides the initial digital model, shared database, and collaborative framework that later stages add on top of [N1-F1][N1-F2].

The transition from BIM to Digital Twin is supported by the fact that BIM is already widely used in design, construction, and operation [N1-F1]. The taxonomy is built on the building life cycle, so the transition is not just a one-time model upgrade but a **lifecycle progression** from design through operation and maintenance [N1-F1]. The authors also note that most prior studies have not fully realized the envisioned Digital Twin, so they classify them under earlier ladder categories [N1-F1]. This reinforces that BIM supports higher levels by providing the foundational model and collaborative infrastructure that later stages build upon [N1-F1][N1-F2].

---

## 4. Organizational and technical barriers in the transition

The evidence indicates several **organizational and technical barriers** in the transition from BIM to Digital Twin.

### Technical barriers
- **Interoperability**: The review notes that information exchange strategies are needed for interoperability across all lifecycle stages [N1-F1]. This is a major technical barrier because BIM must support cross-disciplinary and cross-system data exchange.
- **Data quality and synchronization**: Live data and real-time feedback require high-quality data and tight synchronization between the physical and virtual worlds [N5-F3].
- **AI integration**: Moving to artificial intelligence requires not only data quality but also robust analytics pipelines, machine learning capabilities, and feedback loops [N5-F3].
- **Sensor and IoT integration**: Level 3 depends on connecting BIM to IoT devices, which introduces new technical challenges in data acquisition, transmission, and synchronization [N1-F1][N5-F3].

### Organizational barriers
- **Collaboration and change management**: BIM already supports collaboration, but the transition to Digital Twin requires more extensive cross-organizational and cross-functional coordination [N1-F1][N1-F2].
- **Organizational readiness**: The taxonomy helps explain Digital Twin maturity, but the evidence also suggests that many prior studies are still in earlier ladder categories [N1-F1]. This implies that organizational barriers may include resistance to change, lack of cross-disciplinary collaboration, and difficulty in aligning different systems and processes [N1-F1][N5-F3].

---

## 5. How the taxonomy helps explain Digital Twin maturity

The taxonomy is a useful way to explain **Digital Twin maturity** because it frames the transition as a **lifecycle progression** rather than a single point in time [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The authors’ proposal for an **advanced Digital Twin for building management** shows that the taxonomy is meant to map maturity, not prescribe a single endpoint [N1-F2]. The evidence also states that studies are classified into ladder categories based on how far they have progressed, which means the taxonomy can be used to assess where a project sits in the Digital Twin maturity curve [N1-F1].

In practical terms, the taxonomy helps explain maturity by showing that higher levels require more:
- live data and real-time feedback
- simulation and predictive capability
- AI and analytics
- cross-organizational and cross-system interoperability
- full lifecycle synchronization and control [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F3]

So, maturity is not just about having a Digital Twin; it is about how far along the BIM-to-Digital-Twin ladder a system has progressed [N1-F1][N1-F2].

---

## 6. Alternative taxonomies and why they matter

The evidence shows that several **alternative taxonomies** exist, and they pose a risk of confusion with the BIM-to-Digital-Twin five-level ladder [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R4][N3-R5][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R4][N6-R5]. The most common alternatives include:

- **5-Dimensions models**, which describe digital twins in terms of functionality ranging from static to predictive [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5].
- **5-levels maturity models**, which are maturity-based rather than lifecycle-based and often include stages such as look-alike, static, dynamic, interactive, and extended [N6-R1][N6-R4][N6-R5].
- **System-architecture taxonomies**, which describe digital twins as a layered system with development layers such as data acquisition, data transmission, and other technical layers [N5-R1].

These alternatives differ from the BIM ladder because:
- They are not explicitly tied to the **building life cycle** or **BIM as the first level** [N1-F1][N1-F2].
- They may focus on **functionality**, **maturity**, or **technical architecture** rather than the **BIM-to-Digital-Twin transition** [N3-R1][N3-R2][N6-R1][N6-R4].
- They can be confused with the BIM ladder if one assumes that all “five-level” or “five-dimensional” frameworks are lifecycle-based [N1-F1][N1-F2].

This is important because confusing the BIM ladder with a maturity model or a dimension-based taxonomy can lead to misinterpretation of what the taxonomy is meant to capture [N1-F1][N1-F2][N3-R1][N3-R2][N6-R1][N6-R4].

---

## Conclusion

The five-level ladder taxonomy describes the transition from **BIM** to **Digital Twin** as a **lifecycle progression** through five stages:

1. **BIM** – the foundational digital model and collaborative platform
2. **BIM-supported simulations** – simulation and analysis
3. **BIM integrated with IoT** – live data and real-time feedback
4. **BIM integrated with artificial intelligence** – AI-driven analysis and prediction
5. **advanced Digital Twin** – full lifecycle synchronization and control

The key characteristics are increasing **data quality**, **model fidelity**, **collaboration**, **interoperability**, and **real-time feedback**, with live data and simulation becoming progressively more central [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F3]. BIM is the lowest level and the foundation for higher levels, and the taxonomy helps explain Digital Twin maturity by showing where a project sits along the ladder [N1-F1][N1-F2].

The evidence also warns that alternative taxonomies such as **5-Dimensions**, **5-levels maturity**, and **operational-level** models can be confusing if treated as equivalent to the BIM-to-Digital-Twin ladder [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5][N6-R1][N6-R4]. The safest interpretation is that the BIM ladder is a **building lifecycle-based taxonomy**, while other taxonomies are **functionality-based**, **maturity-based**, or **system-architecture-based** [N1-F1][N1-F2][N3-R1][N6-R1].
